summary: Flama is a web application that turns two decades of NASA FIRMS active fire data into a single, consistent burning activity calendar for Brazil. MODIS and VIIRS detect fires at different resolutions and sensitivities, so their records cannot be compared directly, and MODIS is nearing the end of its operational life. Flama harmonizes both with a conversion factor for each 0.25° grid cell, calibrated on the 2018–2025 overlap; in 2022–2025 validation, the error against observed VIIRS drops from 69% to 15%. One or more areas of interest can be defined by drawing on the map, entering coordinates, uploading property boundaries or selecting states, each monitored separately. The application presents an accessible monthly calendar, the typical fire season, anomalies against multi-year baselines, year-by-year comparisons and the current month relative to the historical median, alongside real-time VIIRS monitoring with area-based alerts. All charts and data are downloadable. This matters because Brazil faces some of the world’s largest fire seasons, with impacts on the Amazon, Cerrado and Pantanal, public health and agriculture. A consistent long-term record allows emergency managers, researchers and landowners to recognize abnormal activity early, anticipate critical periods and prioritize prevention and response.
details:
Flama turns more than two decades of NASA FIRMS active fire detections into one consistent burning activity calendar for Brazil, and pairs it with near-real-time monitoring.

The work has two parts:

  1. Harmonization. MODIS (Terra/Aqua, Collection 6.1, 2000–2025) and VIIRS NOAA-20 (375 m, 2018–present) detections are filtered (vegetation fires only; MODIS confidence ≥ 30; VIIRS nominal/high confidence) and aggregated into monthly counts on a 0.25° grid. For each cell, a conversion factor k (VIIRS ÷ MODIS) is estimated over the April 2018–December 2025 overlap. Cells with few detections borrow strength from their 2° parent region and from the national value through hierarchical shrinkage, which keeps factors stable where data is sparse. Before April 2018 the series is k × MODIS; after that it is VIIRS. The result is a single VIIRS-equivalent record from 2000 to the present. In an out-of-sample test (calibrated on 2018–2021, evaluated on 2022–2025), the monthly error against observed VIIRS falls from 69% with raw MODIS to 18% with a single national factor and 15% with the hierarchical method.
    • a hotspot intensity map;
    • a monthly calendar heatmap;
    • anomalies against the multi-year median or mean;
    • year-by-year comparisons;
    • the typical fire season (start, end and peak month);
    • raw versus harmonized time series;
    • the validation results.

      The monitoring section and downloads include:
    • real-time VIIRS NRT detections (NOAA-20, NOAA-21 and S-NPP) from the last 24 hours, queried from the FIRMS API;
    • automatic refresh at a configurable interval;
    • alerts when new hotspots appear inside any monitored area, each area tracked separately;
    • CSV downloads of calendars, monthly series, hotspot lists (with each detection’s harmonized weight) and alert histories;
    • PNG export of every chart.

Benefits and intended impact

Brazil has some of the largest fire seasons in the world, affecting the Amazon, Cerrado and Pantanal, public health and agriculture. A consistent long-term record answers the questions emergency managers ask most often: which months and years burn the most, whether the current month is above normal, and when the critical season starts in a given place. Combining history with live detections and alerts lets fire brigades, environmental agencies, researchers and landowners recognize abnormal activity early, anticipate critical periods and prioritize prevention and response.

Tools and technologies

  • Language: Python.
  • Data processing: pandas, NumPy, DuckDB (fast queries over Parquet files) and Shapely (geometry operations).
  • Interface: Streamlit, with Folium/Leaflet for the interactive map and drawing tools, and Plotly for charts.
  • Data: NASA FIRMS archives and the FIRMS area API; IBGE state boundaries.
  • Development and hosting: GitHub and Streamlit Community Cloud.
  • Hardware: standard laptop; no specialized hardware.

Creativity

  • Spatially varying harmonization: instead of a single global correction, the factor adapts to each 0.25° cell and is stabilized hierarchically where data is sparse, which captures regional differences in how the two sensors see fire.
  • Fair comparison of the current month: when the month is still in progress, only the same days of previous years are compared (for example, 1–15 November), avoiding misleading drops.
  • Property-level monitoring: official land-registry boundaries can be uploaded directly, and multiple properties can be monitored separately, bringing satellite data to the scale at which landowners and local managers act.

Factors considered

  • Accessibility: colorblind-safe palettes (YlOrRd, RdBu, Okabe-Ito), signs and arrows in addition to color, and a bilingual interface (English/Portuguese) with light and dark themes.
    • avoiding double counting in the MODIS/VIIRS overlap;
    • flagging that only Terra operated in 2000–2002;
    • keeping real-time detections clearly separated from the harmonized series, since NRT data is raw and arrives about three hours after each satellite pass.
  • Practical constraints: data split into compact yearly Parquet files for free hosting, API keys kept out of the code, and caching to respect FIRMS request limits.
    • automated daily updates of the historical series;
    • expansion beyond Brazil, since the method is region-agnostic;
    • integration with ground-reported fire records.
